Cloud Readiness

Issue CategoryCriticalityStory Point
HttpSession state requires sticky sessions in cloud deployments
 Mandatory 5
FilePosition
src/main/java/com/zavabank/compliancereporter/AuthFilter.javaLine 26
src/main/java/com/zavabank/compliancereporter/LoginServlet.javaLine 29
src/main/java/com/zavabank/compliancereporter/ReportsServlet.javaLine 22

Explanation

The application stores authentication state (SessionUser) in HttpSession. In a horizontally-scaled cloud environment, requests from the same user may be routed to different instances, losing session state. Sticky sessions (session affinity) must be configured, or session state must be moved to an external store (e.g., Redis, Azure Cache).

src/main/resources/compliance.propertiesLine 5

Explanation

The compliance.properties file contains plaintext database credentials (db.user=sa, db.password) committed to source control. Credentials must be removed from version control and injected at runtime via a secret store (Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets) or environment variables sourced from a secure pipeline.
JDBC DriverManager used without a connection pool
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/main/java/com/zavabank/compliancereporter/ComplianceConnectionFactory.javaLine 15

Explanation

The application calls DriverManager.getConnection() directly on every request without a connection pool. Under load this can exhaust database connections and degrade performance. A connection pooling library such as HikariCP should be introduced before cloud deployment.
java.net.HttpURLConnection used for external service calls without retry or circuit breaker
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/main/java/com/zavabank/compliancereporter/SsoSessionService.javaLine 76

Explanation

SsoSessionService uses java.net.HttpURLConnection with hardcoded 3-second timeouts to call the ZavaBank Auth Gateway. There is no retry logic, circuit breaker, or fallback beyond an empty-string return. In a cloud environment, transient network failures can cause authentication to fail silently.

 Optional 5

Explanation

The application is packaged as a WAR file deployed to an external Tomcat container. Modern cloud-native applications use an embedded server model (Spring Boot, Quarkus) for simpler containerisation, faster startup, and easier configuration management.

Architecture Diagram

ZavaComplianceReporter is a Java 8 Servlet/JSP web application deployed on Apache Tomcat 9 that enables bank compliance officers to generate and download CTR (Currency Transaction Reports) and SAR (Suspicious Activity Reports) backed by a Microsoft SQL Server database.

Data Storage & External Services

The sole data store is a Microsoft SQL Server instance (ZavaBankDB) accessed via plain JDBC with DriverManager.getConnection. The schema includes ComplianceReports, Transactions, Accounts, FraudAlerts, SessionTokens, and Users tables. There is no connection pool or ORM layer.

The only external service is the ZavaBank Auth Gateway (a .NET ASP.NET application), which exposes a WhoAmI.ashx endpoint. SsoSessionService calls this endpoint over HTTP to exchange the .ZAVAAUTH FormsAuthentication cookie for a Java-readable session token when the cookie-based SSO path is used.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Servlet-centric MVC without a framework: The application uses raw HttpServlet subclasses and JSP templates instead of a modern web framework (Spring MVC, JAX-RS). Controllers are tightly coupled to the HTTP layer.
  • Session-based authentication via HttpSession: After token validation, the resolved SessionUser is stored in the HTTP session, requiring sticky sessions (session affinity) in any horizontally-scaled cloud deployment.
  • Classpath properties with environment-variable override: ComplianceConfig loads compliance.properties from the classpath but checks environment variables first, providing a basic externalisation mechanism.

Communication Patterns

Synchronous only. The application has no message queues, event-driven patterns, or asynchronous processing.

Inbound: Browser → Tomcat HTTP (port 8080). No HTTPS/TLS termination is configured at the application level; TLS would need to be handled by a reverse proxy or load balancer in front of Tomcat.

Outbound to SQL Server: Direct JDBC using DriverManager.getConnection() called per-request with no connection pool. Timeout is governed by the MSSQL JDBC driver defaults; no explicit timeout, retry, or circuit-breaker policy is configured.

Outbound to Auth Gateway: SsoSessionService.resolveTokenFromAuthGateway() uses java.net.HttpURLConnection with a 3-second connect timeout and 3-second read timeout (setConnectTimeout(3000), setReadTimeout(3000)). There is no retry logic, circuit breaker, or fallback — if the gateway is unreachable the method returns an empty string and authentication falls through to a database token lookup. Service discovery is absent; the gateway URL is hardcoded in auth.gateway.whoami.url configuration.

Security posture: The /reports, /reports/generate, and /reports/download paths are protected by AuthFilter, which validates the HTTP session and redirects unauthenticated requests to /login. The /health and /login endpoints are publicly accessible with no authentication. No TLS is configured at the application layer. Authorization is coarse-grained (presence of a valid SessionUser in the session) with no role-based access control (RBAC) or @PreAuthorize-style permission checks.

Service discovery: None. Both the SQL Server host and the auth-gateway URL are resolved from static configuration (compliance.properties or environment variables).

Startup dependencies: The application depends on SQL Server and the auth gateway being reachable at start-up (connection opened on first request). There is no startup health-check mechanism beyond the /health endpoint, which does not verify downstream dependencies.

Startup Dependency Chain

The application has no explicit startup health-check or dependency-wait mechanism. Services are expected to be available before the container starts processing requests:

  1. SQL Server (ZavaBankDB) — must be reachable before any request that queries the database. No dockerize wait, no readiness probe beyond the custom /health endpoint (which does NOT verify DB connectivity).
  2. ZavaBank Auth Gateway (WhoAmI.ashx) — must be reachable for SSO via .ZAVAAUTH cookie. A 3-second connect/read timeout is hardcoded; failure falls through to a direct session-token DB lookup.
  3. Tomcat 9 — starts with no precondition checks; first failure is reported at request time, not at startup.

There is no Docker Compose depends_on, Kubernetes readiness probe verifying downstream services, or Spring Cloud Config retry policy.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Current state: Secrets are provisioned by embedding plaintext values in compliance.properties (committed to the repository) or by injecting them as plain environment variables at container startup. There is no formal secrets provisioning workflow — no managed identity, no RBAC-scoped Key Vault access, and no CI/CD pipeline secret binding.

Recommended direction for cloud deployment:

  • Remove db.password, db.user, and auth.gateway.whoami.url from the committed properties file.
  • Inject sensitive values at runtime via environment variables sourced from a secret store (e.g., Azure Key Vault via a managed identity, or Kubernetes Secrets mounted as env vars).
  • Grant the application a least-privilege database account (not sa).
  • Enforce TLS on the auth gateway URL.

Core Business Workflows

ZavaComplianceReporter enables bank compliance officers to generate, review, and download regulatory filings — specifically Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — submitted to FinCEN as part of the Bank Secrecy Act compliance program.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: SSO Authentication

A compliance officer arrives at the application and must prove their identity before accessing compliance reports. Authentication is handled by AuthFilter (for protected routes) and LoginServlet (for the login page).

Steps:

  1. Officer navigates to /reports (protected route). AuthFilter checks whether a valid SessionUser is present in the HTTP session.
  2. If no session exists, SsoSessionService attempts to resolve a session token from three sources (in priority order):

a. Explicit sessionToken form/query parameter

b. X-Session-Token HTTP header or `Authorization: header

c. .ZAVAAUTH cookie — if found, the auth gateway (WhoAmI.ashx) is called to exchange the FormsAuth cookie for a Java-readable session token

  1. The resolved token is validated against SessionTokens and Users in SQL Server. The token must be active (IsActive=1), not expired (ExpiresAt > GETDATE()), and the owning user must be active.
  2. On success, a SessionUser (userId, username) is stored in HttpSession and the request continues. On failure, the officer is redirected to /login.

Workflow 2: Generate Currency Transaction Report (CTR)

A compliance officer generates a CTR listing all transactions above a configurable dollar threshold, as required by the Bank Secrecy Act for transactions of $10,000 or more.

Steps:

  1. Officer selects "Generate CTR" on the reports page and submits a threshold amount (default: $10,000.00).
  2. GenerateReportServlet validates the threshold (falls back to $10,000.00 if invalid).
  3. The application queries Transactions joined with Accounts for all transactions where ABS(Amount) >= threshold, ordered by date descending (TOP 200).
  4. A plain-text CTR report document is assembled with transaction ID, account number, amount, date, and description for each matching row.
  5. The report is inserted into ComplianceReports with ReportType='CTR', Status='Generated', RegulatoryBody='FinCEN', and the filing officer's username.
  6. The officer is redirected to the reports list where the new entry appears.

Workflow 3: Generate Suspicious Activity Report (SAR)

A compliance officer generates a SAR capturing all unresolved or high-severity fraud alerts, as required when suspicious financial activity is detected.

Steps:

  1. Officer selects "Generate SAR" on the reports page and submits the form.
  2. The application queries FraudAlerts where Severity IN ('High', 'Critical') OR Status IN ('New', 'InReview'), ordered by creation date descending (TOP 200).
  3. A plain-text SAR report document is assembled with alert ID, transaction ID, severity, status, date, and description.
  4. The report is inserted into ComplianceReports with ReportType='SAR', same status and regulatory body as CTR.
  5. The officer is redirected to the reports list.

Workflow 4: View and Download Compliance Reports

Steps:

  1. Officer navigates to /reports. ReportsServlet queries the 100 most recent ComplianceReports, ordered by filing date descending.
  2. The reports list (ID, type, date, status, filed-by) is rendered in the browser as an HTML table.
  3. To download a report, the officer clicks "Download" for a specific ReportID. DownloadReportServlet retrieves the stored report text and streams it as a text/plain file attachment named {ReportType}-{ReportID}.txt.

Cross-Service Data Flows

ZavaComplianceReporter is a single-service monolith with one external dependency:

Cookie-to-Token Exchange (SSO flow):

When a .ZAVAAUTH FormsAuthentication cookie is present, the application calls the ZavaBank Auth Gateway's WhoAmI.ashx endpoint over HTTP (3-second timeout), passing the cookie. The gateway returns a JSON response containing a sessionToken field. This token is then validated in-process against the local SessionTokens table. If the gateway call fails or times out, the application falls back to checking the sessionToken query parameter and then the X-Session-Token header before giving up.

There is no other cross-service data aggregation. All compliance data (transactions, accounts, fraud alerts) lives in the same SQL Server database and is accessed directly.

Business Workflow Sequence

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation Rules

RuleWhere AppliedLogic
CTR threshold validityGenerateReportServlet.parseThresholdIf the submitted thresholdAmount cannot be parsed as a BigDecimal, it defaults to $10,000.00
Report type whitelistGenerateReportServlet.doPostOnly CTR and SAR are accepted (case-insensitive); any other value redirects to /reports with no report generated
Report ID validityDownloadReportServlet.doGetIf reportId cannot be parsed as an integer or no matching row exists, the officer is redirected to /reports
Session token requirementsSsoSessionService.resolveSessionUserToken must exist in SessionTokens, have IsActive=1, have ExpiresAt > GETDATE(), and belong to a Users row with IsActive=1

Decision Logic — Authentication Token Resolution Priority

SsoSessionService resolves a session token using the following priority chain (first non-empty value wins):

  1. Explicit sessionToken form/query parameter
  2. X-Session-Token HTTP header
  3. `Authorization: header
  4. .ZAVAAUTH cookie → call Auth Gateway → extract sessionToken from JSON response

If no token is found via any path, authentication fails and the officer is redirected to the login page.

SAR Alert Inclusion Criteria

A FraudAlert is included in a SAR if either condition holds:

  • Severity IN ('High', 'Critical') — high-risk alerts regardless of status
  • Status IN ('New', 'InReview') — unresolved alerts regardless of severity

This union logic means a low-severity alert that is still open will be included in the SAR, and a closed high-severity alert will also be included.

State Transitions

ComplianceReport has a simple lifecycle: all reports are created with Status='Generated'. No state transition logic (e.g., "Submitted → Acknowledged → Accepted") is implemented — status updates would need to be performed externally (directly in the database).

Audit & Logging

FiledBy (the authenticated officer's username) and CreatedDate are recorded on each ComplianceReport at insert time, providing a basic audit trail of who generated each filing. No application-level audit log, change history, or event log is maintained beyond this database record.

Authorization

Authorization is coarse-grained: any authenticated user (any valid session token mapped to an active Users row) can generate, view, and download any compliance report. There is no role hierarchy (e.g., analyst vs supervisor), no resource-ownership check (e.g., "only the filing officer can download their own reports"), and no approval workflow for submitted filings.

Transaction Boundaries

No explicit transaction management is applied. Each JDBC Connection is opened in auto-commit mode, meaning each SQL statement is committed immediately. A failure during CTR/SAR report generation (e.g., after data is assembled but before INSERT completes) does not trigger a rollback.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The most significant risk is the javax namespace. Both javax.servlet-api:3.1.0 (provided by Tomcat 9) and javax.servlet:jstl:1.2 use the javax. package namespace, which was renamed to jakarta. in Jakarta EE 9 (Tomcat 10+). Migrating to a modern container runtime requires replacing both with their Jakarta equivalents (jakarta.servlet-api and org.glassfish.web:jakarta.tags / jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl). The mssql-jdbc:12.8.1.jre8 artifact is current as of the build date but targets JRE 8; switching to a JRE 11+ or JRE 17+ variant (.jre11 / .jre17) is required when the runtime is upgraded. The entire project targets Java 8 (sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_1_8), which reached end of standard Oracle support in March 2022; upgrading to Java 21 LTS is strongly recommended.

Notable Observations

  • No HTTP client library declared: The application makes outbound HTTP calls to the auth gateway using only the built-in java.net.HttpURLConnection, with no retry, circuit-breaker, or connection pool logic. Adding a modern HTTP client (e.g., Apache HttpClient 5 or OkHttp) would improve resilience.
  • No connection pooling library: Direct DriverManager.getConnection() is used for every database operation. A connection pool (e.g., HikariCP) is absent and should be introduced before cloud deployment to avoid connection exhaustion under load.
  • No logging framework declared: There is no SLF4J, Log4j 2, or Logback dependency. The application relies on caught-and-ignored exceptions (catch (Exception ignored)), making it impossible to observe failures in production.
  • Minimal dependency footprint: Only 3 declared dependencies make the migration surface small, but the absence of modern abstractions (frameworks, pooling, logging) means significant manual work is needed to achieve cloud readiness.

Test Dependencies

No test-scoped dependencies detected.

Total test-scope dependencies: 0

No test framework (JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ, etc.) is declared in build.gradle. The project has no unit or integration test infrastructure, which will make validating any migration changes more difficult and increases the risk of regressions.

ZavaComplianceReporter uses a single Microsoft SQL Server database (ZavaBankDB) accessed entirely through raw JDBC — there is no ORM, no connection pool, and no schema migration tool. The data layer spans 6 inferred tables across compliance reporting, transaction processing, fraud management, and identity.

Key Repository Methods

There are no formal repository interfaces. All data access is performed inline within Servlet methods via ComplianceConnectionFactory.openConnection(). The table below documents the effective query operations:

AND st.IsActive=1 AND st.ExpiresAt > GETDATE() AND u.IsActive=1 ORDER BY st.ExpiresAt DESCSessionTokens, UsersAuthenticate a session token and return the owning user

Transaction management: No explicit transaction management (@Transactional or Connection.setAutoCommit(false)) is used. Each Connection is opened in auto-commit mode (JDBC default). Partial failures within a single request are not rolled back.

Caching Strategy

No caching layer is configured. There is no Redis, EhCache, Caffeine, or Spring Cache (@Cacheable) in the project. All data is read directly from SQL Server on every request. HTTP session storage (HttpSession) is used exclusively for user identity, not for query result caching.

Data Ownership Boundaries

All tables reside in a single shared SQL Server instance (ZavaBankDB). There is no database-per-service separation, no schema-per-service partitioning, and no logical ownership boundary enforced at the data layer. The application is the sole writer and reader of all tables.

Cross-service data access is limited to the outbound HTTP call to the ZavaBank Auth Gateway for cookie-to-token resolution; no database-level cross-service access occurs. Session token validation is performed directly against the SessionTokens and Users tables in the same database.

Read/write patterns are simple request-scoped reads and writes — there is no CQRS separation, read replica, or eventual consistency concern.

Summary: The application processes and stores PCI-relevant financial data and PII for a FinCEN-regulated compliance workflow. No encryption-at-rest, field-level masking, data-loss prevention, or audit logging is in place. Session tokens are stored and transmitted in plaintext, creating a credential-theft risk. These gaps must be addressed prior to any cloud deployment.
